Outcome-heterogeneity guard: DAI spans Adams grade I-III and the literature records both substantial recovery and permanent deficit; the claim is scoped to documented DAI with neuropsychological testing at least 6-12 months post-injury, once spontaneous recovery has plateaued.

Competing-cause guard: hypoxic-ischemic injury, secondary brain damage, hydrocephalus, and post-traumatic hypopituitarism produce overlapping cognitive deficits and must be excluded before the DAI pathway carries individual weight.
governanceNotes: Authored at DIRECT_CAUSATION with PROBABLE consensus and hypothesizedOnly:false, following the cerebral-contusion -> seizure-disorder structural-lesion precedent: the expert neuropsychology overview attributes the moderate-to-severe TBI cognitive-deficit syndrome to diffuse axonal injury explicitly (Azouvi 2017), and the DAI pathology chapter documents connectivity disruption as a cause of long-term disability (Su & Bell 2016).

The claim is scoped to documented DAI (MRI/DTI findings or grade at presentation) with neuropsychological confirmation of the deficit pattern; it is not a nexus probability assertion for any individual claim.

nexusClaim.etiologicalTrigger: Documented diffuse axonal injury (grade I-III or MRI/DTI-confirmed axonal shearing) -> widespread disruption of cerebral connectivity across corpus callosum, parasagittal white matter, and brainstem -> neuropsychologically confirmed cognitive deficits (processing speed, memory, attention, executive function) persisting beyond the spontaneous-recovery window.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A connectivity-disruption pathway: acceleration/deceleration torque shears axons at the corpus callosum, parasagittal white matter, and brainstem; axonal disconnection and secondary Wallerian degeneration impair integration across distributed networks governing processing speed, memory encoding, attention, and executive control; the deficit syndrome corresponds to the disrupted networks rather than a focal lesion, and recovery reflects partial reorganization rather than axonal regrowth. Secondary injury (edema, ischemia) can extend the axonal loss, so acute-severity documentation is required.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: The expert neuropsychology literature attributes the moderate-to-severe TBI cognitive-deficit syndrome to diffuse axonal injury, and the pathology literature documents DAI as a cause of long-term disability in 40%-50% of TBI admissions; the mechanism is the established consequence of axonal shearing and the claim is scoped to documented DAI with neuropsychological confirmation. Consensus is PROBABLE for the scoped structural claim; it is not a nexus probability assertion for any individual claim.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: acute-imaging documentation of DAI (MRI with DTI/SWI, or grade at presentation) and injury severity (GCS, PTA duration); neuropsychological testing at least 6-12 months post-injury identifying the deficit pattern; chronology from injury to deficits; exclusion of hypoxic-ischemic injury, hydrocephalus, medication effects, and post-traumatic hypopituitarism (endocrine evaluation where indicated)
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Hypoxic-ischemic brain injury from circulatory or respiratory arrest
Post-traumatic hypopituitarism (overlapping cognitive and mood symptoms)
Medication and sedative effects during the testing period

sourceReferences.citation: Azouvi P, Arnould A, Dromer E, Vallat-Azouvi C. Neuropsychology of traumatic brain injury: An expert overview. Rev Neurol (Paris). 2017;173(7-8):461-472. PMID 28847474.
sourceReferences.note: Expert overview: patients who survive moderate-to-severe TBI frequently suffer a wide range of cognitive deficits and behavioral changes due to diffuse axonal injury - slowed information processing, impaired long-term memory, attention, working memory, executive function, social cognition, and self-awareness; mental fatigue frequently exacerbates the deficits.
sourceReferences.sourceLocator: PMID 28847474; cognitive deficits attributed to diffuse axonal injury

sourceReferences.citation: Su E, Bell M. Diffuse Axonal Injury. In: Translational Research in Traumatic Brain Injury. CRC Press/Taylor and Francis; 2016. PMID 26583181.
sourceReferences.note: DAI review chapter: widespread axonal damage produces deficits in cerebral connectivity that may or may not recover; DAI is a component of injury in 40%-50% of TBI hospital admissions, commonly affecting brainstem, parasagittal white matter, and corpus callosum, and is increasingly recognized as an important cause of long-term disability.
sourceReferences.sourceLocator: PMID 26583181; connectivity-disruption mechanism and 40-50% admission share

sourceReferences.citation: Pavlovic D, Pekic S, Stojanovic M, Popovic V. Traumatic brain injury: neuropathological, neurocognitive and neurobehavioral sequelae. Pituitary. 2019;22(3):270-282. PMID 30929221.
sourceReferences.note: Sequelae review: DAI is visible only with advanced neuroimaging (DTI for white-matter pathology, SWI for microbleeds); chronic TBI patients have lower neuropsychological scores and higher mental-distress symptoms; TBI-related hypopituitarism overlaps with and can mimic cognitive disability - recorded as a competing cause requiring endocrine evaluation.
